title: Operators, precedence and formatted I/O
subtitle: Expressions are evaluated in a fixed order. Know it, and you can predict any line of arithmetic before the computer does.

sections.title: Arithmetic operators
sections.body:
Ready for a surprise? Ask C what 7/2 is and it will say 3. Not 3.5. Three. Is the computer bad at maths? No, it is following a rule, and the rule is the whole lesson.

You get the usual + - * / plus the remainder %. With two integers, / is integer division: it truncates, throwing away the fraction. And % gives the leftover, so 7 % 3 is 1. Want the honest 3.5? Make one operand a double: 7/2.0. The type of the operands decides what kind of division happens.

figures.caption: Figure 3.1.1 — Arithmetic operators

keynotes: With two integers, / is integer division and truncates: 7/2 is 3, not 3.5.
% gives the remainder: 7 % 3 is 1.
To get 3.5 make one operand a double (7/2.0).

sections.title: Precedence and associativity
sections.body:
What is 2 + 3 * 4? If you said 14, you already know C’s secret: some operators are more eager than others, and multiplication goes before addition. This ordering is called precedence, and it is the order in which an expression is quietly taken apart.

From high to low: parentheses, unary (! - ++ --), * / %, + -, relational (< > <= >=), equality (== !=), &&, ||, assignment. When two operators tie, they go left to right (assignment is the exception, right to left). And the golden rule: when unsure, add parentheses. Nobody ever lost marks for clarity.

Try one together: 2 + 3 * 4 − 6 / 2. Multiplication and division first, giving 12 and 3, so the line becomes 2 + 12 − 3. Then left to right: 11. Do the same by hand for the question below before you peek.

figures.caption: Figure 3.2.1 — Precedence and associativity

keynotes: Precedence from high to low: parentheses, unary, * / %, + -, relational, equality, &&, ||, assignment.
Equal precedence goes left to right; assignment goes right to left.
When unsure, add parentheses.
2 + 3 * 4 − 6 / 2 becomes 2 + 12 − 3, which is 11.

sections.title: Increment, compound assignment, conversion
sections.body:
Programmers are lazy in a good way, so C has shortcuts. x += 5 means x = x + 5. And then there are the two flavours of increment, which trip up everybody once: i++ uses i then adds 1, while ++i adds 1 then uses it. Post-increment yields the old value, pre-increment the new one. Check the figure to see it happen.

Mixed types? In a mixed expression the smaller type is promoted (int → double) so nothing is lost. And if you want to force it yourself, use a cast: (double)a / b. Try the question below, and see whether you can say what j will be before reading any further.

questions.prompt: int i = 2; int j = i++ + 3; leaves j =

figures.caption: Figure 3.3.1 — Increment, compound assignment, conversion
figures.note: Post-increment yields the old value; pre-increment the new one.

keynotes: x += 5 means x = x + 5.
i++ uses i then adds 1 (yielding the old value); ++i adds 1 then uses it (yielding the new one).
In mixed expressions the smaller type is promoted (int → double); a cast such as (double)a / b forces it.

sections.title: Relational, logical and bitwise
sections.body:
How does C represent true and false? With numbers: 0 is false and any non-zero is true, and comparisons yield 0 or 1. Simple, a little strange, and very useful.

Here is a trick that protects your programs. && and || short-circuit: they stop as soon as the answer is known. In a != 0 && x/a > 1, when a is 0 the first test fails, so the division is never attempted. That is exactly why p != NULL && *p > 0 is safe. The guard comes first.

Then there are bitwise operators, & | ^ ~ << >>, which work on the bits themselves: x << 1 doubles an integer. Try AND by hand: 12 = 1100₂, 10 = 1010₂. Go bit by bit, and 1100 & 1010 gives 1000₂, which is 8.

choices.text: && short-circuits, so *p is skipped when p is NULL.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Right side is evaluated only if the left is true.

keynotes: In C, 0 is false and any non-zero is true; comparisons yield 0 or 1.
&& and || short-circuit, so a != 0 && x/a > 1 never divides when a is 0.
Bitwise operators work on bits: x << 1 doubles an integer.
12 AND 10 (1100₂ and 1010₂) is 1000₂, which is 8.

sections.title: printf and scanf
sections.body:
A program that cannot talk to anyone is not much use. Two functions do most of the talking, and you will use them in almost every program. printf("fmt", args) writes formatted output, using conversion specifiers: %d int, %f double/float, %c char, %s string, %x hex. And %5.2f means width 5, 2 decimals.

Then scanf("%d", &n) reads input, and look hard at that little &. scanf needs the variable’s address so it can store into it. Without the address it would be handed a copy of n and could change nothing. Input flows into memory; output flows from it. For single characters there are getchar and putchar.

choices.text: It must know where in memory to store the value.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: C passes by value, so the address is passed.

figures.caption: Figure 4.1.1 — scanf then printf
figures.note: Input flows into memory; output flows from it.

keynotes: printf writes formatted output using specifiers: %d int, %f double/float, %c char, %s string, %x hex.
%5.2f means width 5 with 2 decimals.
scanf needs the variable’s address (&n) so it can store into it.
getchar and putchar handle single characters.

sections.title: Format specifiers at a glance
sections.body:
Here is a cheat-sheet to keep at your elbow. Don’t memorise it; use it until it sticks.

SpecMeaningprintf(…) gives
%dint42 → 42
%5dwidth 542 → ···42
%.2f2 decimals3.14159 → 3.14
%cchar65 → A
%sstring"hi" → hi

Notice how a number is just a number until the specifier tells printf how to dress it: 65 becomes the letter A when you ask for %c.
keynotes: %d prints an int and %5d pads it to width 5.
%.2f prints 2 decimals, so 3.14159 gives 3.14.
%c prints a char (65 gives A) and %s prints a string.
